policy.sourceOfTruth: DNR official park, 2025 visitor guide and official trail descriptions; parking IDs from existing DNR crosswalk
policy.visitorNotice: These are outings to compare, not GPS routes. A named trail does not prove an open gate, passable bridge or accessible parking.
policy.photoEvidenceRule: Photographs are exact park or destination context with verified public-domain/Commons reuse, not confirmation of an individual trail entrance, route, facility layout, season, or current conditions. Any site-wide or historic image must explicitly state its limited scope.

options.name: Lake of the Clouds overlook
options.tagline: The world opens over the escarpment.
options.accessSurface: DNR describes roughly 100 yards of paved trail or accessible boardwalk to the overlook.
options.publishedDistance: Overlook approach: approximately 100 yards (DNR 2025 visitor guide). Not the Escarpment Trail.
options.experience: A wide view of Lake of the Clouds and the old-growth valley without committing to a long ridge hike.
options.limits: The longer Escarpment Trail begins in this district but is a separate strenuous outing. M-107 scenic-road gates are seasonal. RV/trailer staging is not this upper lot.

photo.alt: Lake of the Clouds beneath the wooded escarpment in autumn
photo.credit: Lake of the Clouds · Stevenliuyi · CC BY-SA 4.0

options.photoAbout: Actual Lake of the Clouds overlook; archival photo, not a current conditions view.
options.fieldNote: The view begins with a surprise: Lake of the Clouds lies far below you, enclosed by steep wooded slopes. The Michigan DNR describes this as part of an ancient escarpment stretching across the mountains. Spend a minute looking beyond the water to the unbroken forest in the valley. The short overlook approach offers the scene without committing to the very different, rugged Escarpment Trail.

options.name: Summit Peak tower
options.tagline: A high tower above the hardwoods.
options.accessSurface: Packed dirt approach through hardwood forest, benches, and a tower reached by wooden stairs.
options.publishedDistance: DNR describes 0.5 mile from parking to tower and about 300 feet of climbing. Not a calculated return hike.
options.experience: Follow a forest path before climbing to views across the western Upper Peninsula's hills.
options.limits: Tower stairs are not a step-free overlook. South Boundary Road access is seasonal and the upper parking approach is not appropriate for unverified trailers/RVs.

photo.alt: Viewing platform overlooking forested ridges near Summit Peak trail
photo.credit: Near Summit Peak trail · daveynin · CC BY 4.0 · July 2026

options.photoAbout: Scenic view near Summit Peak trail; not proof of conditions on your chosen date.
options.fieldNote: Take your time under the hardwood canopy on the way to Summit Peak. The half-mile approach and benches are part of the outing, not just a walk to the tower. Climb the wooden stairs, if appropriate for your group, and look for the rolling pattern of forested ridges rather than a single landmark. This is an elevated tower experience, not an accessible roadside platform.

options.name: Presque Isle waterfalls
options.tagline: Hear the river in a dark-rock gorge.
options.accessSurface: Wooden stairs and riverbank boardwalks at the falls; a separate gravel path behind the DNR contact booth provides shorter Nawadaha viewing access.
options.publishedDistance: DNR older trail descriptions: West River 1.1 miles; East River 1.2 miles. They are separate trail descriptions, not a certified loop.
options.experience: A river-country outing among Nawadaha, Manido and Manabezho, with different viewing approaches.
options.limits: Accessible Nawadaha platform does not make the whole river corridor accessible. The contact-booth entrance is NOT matched to parking asset #841. The M-28/CR519 work-zone reopening and last-mile vehicle turns remain unverified.

photo.alt: Manabezho Falls rushing over dark rock ledges on the Presque Isle River

options.photoAbout: Actual Manabezho Falls within the Presque Isle corridor; not a photograph of every falls or trail.
options.fieldNote: Here the Presque Isle River enters a remarkable stretch of old-growth sugar maple, hemlock and white pine. Water runs over lower cascades, then gathers into narrower channels carved deeply through bedrock. Stop and listen before choosing a viewpoint: the sound changes as the gorge tightens. Nawadaha has a separately documented accessible observation platform; the entire river corridor is not an accessible or verified loop.

options.name: Visitor Center Nature Trail
options.tagline: Meet the old forest at its edge.
options.accessSurface: Interpretive nature path near the visitor center; no verified step-free route for the full loop.
options.publishedDistance: DNR trail descriptions list 1.4 miles for the loop; this is a published trail length, not a current verified hike.
options.experience: Follow the park's forest story more quietly, with a chance to explore exhibits when the visitor center is open.
options.limits: Visitor Center building seasonal hours are May 15–Oct 14; closed Oct 15–May 14. Trail access and surface conditions are not confirmed by building hours.

photo.alt: Wooded walking path photographed in Porcupine Mountains Wilderness State Park in 2014; specific Visitor Center Nature Trail entrance not identified
photo.credit: Porkies forest path · Yinan Chen · public domain · 2014
photo.locationVerified: Porcupine Mountains Wilderness State Park; precise Visitor Center Nature Trail identity unverified

options.photoAbout: Real 2014 photograph of a wooded path somewhere in the Porcupine Mountains, NOT confirmed as the Visitor Center Nature Trail or its entrance.
options.fieldNote: The first thing to notice here is the forest itself. Hemlocks hold the shade beneath broad-leaved hardwoods, and the quiet understory gives you a hint of the vast old-growth wilderness farther into the park. When the visitor center is open, its exhibits provide context for the landscape before you walk. The building's seasonal closure does not by itself tell you whether the outdoor nature trail is passable.

options.name: Escarpment Trail
options.tagline: The rugged ridge beyond the easy overlook.
options.accessSurface: Steep exposed ridge hiking with large changes in elevation; a long one-way alignment and return/shuttle planning.
options.publishedDistance: DNR editions disagree: older description 4.3 miles; 2025 GPS map 3.7 miles. Neither is a parking-to-parking trip.
options.experience: Take the longer escarpment above the lake into a more demanding wilderness landscape.
options.limits: Not the 100-yard accessible overlook. DNR crossing/mapping records do not certify an unbroken passable route, return shuttle, or current road access.

photo.alt: Lake of the Clouds beneath the wooded escarpment in autumn
photo.credit: Lake of the Clouds · Stevenliuyi · CC BY-SA 4.0

options.photoAbout: Lake of the Clouds scenic region; photograph is not a documented view from every Escarpment Trail section.
options.fieldNote: From the ridge, the forest and Lake of the Clouds seem to unfold in layers. This is the longer, more physically demanding side of the escarpment, not the short accessible viewing approach. Its age and scale are part of the wonder, but so is its remoteness: trail editions disagree on mileage and the current complete route and return logistics are not certified by this planner. Study the official map before considering a traverse.

options.name: Winter Sports Complex
options.tagline: Follow the snow into the eastern hills.
options.accessSurface: Separate cross-country ski, snowshoe and winter-sport experiences; exact activity access must be confirmed on the official snow report.
options.publishedDistance: The DNR describes a park ski-trail network, but this is not an individual verified skiing itinerary or distance.
options.experience: Snow-covered forest and winter recreation in the eastern park approach instead of closed summer scenic roads.
options.limits: No live snow, lift operations, rental availability or grooming is verified here. Do not assume the building, tracks or lot are open.

photo.alt: Historical 1959 winter skiing photograph made in the Porcupine Mountains; not an image of today's facilities or trail grooming
photo.credit: Porcupine Mountains skiing, March 1959 · Victor Grigas · CC BY-SA 2.0
photo.locationVerified: Photographer's label places historical skiing in Porcupine Mountains; modern Winter Sports Complex entrance and grooming not identified

options.photoAbout: Authentic 1959 Porcupine Mountains skiing archive, NOT today's Winter Sports Complex, current conditions, lift, or grooming.
options.fieldNote: When snow settles across the hills, the Porkies become a different park. Groomed cross-country routes and the winter sports complex offer a way into the eastern forest while some scenic roads are closed to vehicles. Look for the shape of the hardwoods against the snow and listen for the quieter winter woods. The official ski report, not the calendar alone, determines whether any particular activity or lift is operating.
